verdict.reasoning: Patient describes “a bit of chest discomfort… like a pressure on my chest… feels like someone's sitting on my chest” and confirms “No, they're still present.” Location is “in the middle of my chest… quite a diffuse pain.”

Onset: “it started just when I was gardening… I was just kneeling down… it wasn't during any physical exercise.” Persistence at rest is implied by ongoing symptoms: when asked if symptoms are present now, patient says “No, they're still present.”
Patient states: “I've noticed a bit of nausea, not. No vomiting.”
Patient notes: “I'm pretty sweaty,” which corresponds to diaphoresis.
Patient reports being “short of breath” along with the chest discomfort.
When asked about radiation, patient says: “it's mainly my left arm… a little bit painful and in my shoulder as well.”

Patient acknowledges faster heartbeat but denies true palpitations: “Yeah, it's beating a bit faster now… but I haven't noticed it beating faster than usual.” There is no statement that chest discomfort is associated with palpitations.
When asked if he has had this before, patient replies: “No, this is the first time, actually.”
Doctor asks about high blood pressure; patient answers: “Yeah, I have high blood pressure but not diabetes.”
The transcript contains no mention of any current medications, so stating that none are mentioned is accurate.

Patient: “Yes, actually I have an allergy to aspirin.” Describes it as “an allergic reaction… I swallow a bit, but nothing life threatening… it's a mild reaction.” Swelling is reasonably inferred from “I swallow a bit.”
Patient says: “my father died of a heart attack” and clarifies age: “He was about my age… Around 60, yes.” Myocardial infarction is the clinical term for heart attack.
Patient states: “my mother had some heart problems.”
Patient: “I smoke a fair bit. So I smoke about 10 cigarettes a day… For the past 15 years.”
On alcohol: “Probably about seven or eight pints a week… Oh, beer, yes.”
Doctor asks if patient is overweight; patient replies: “Yes, I'm overweight, yeah.”
Living situation: “Yeah, I live alone at the moment. Yeah, it's just me in the house.”
Employment: “I work as a restaurant owner. So I own a sushi shop.”

Symptoms listed (ongoing chest pain/pressure, shortness of breath, sweating, nausea, left arm/shoulder pain) are all in transcript. Doctor explicitly says: “The symptoms that you've described to me, they indicate the possibility of a heart attack… our number one priority to exclude that,” which corresponds to possible acute coronary syndrome.

Risk factors present: hypertension (“I have high blood pressure”), smoking 10/day for 15 years, overweight (“Yes, I'm overweight”), family history of MI at ~60, and male sex about 60 years old. Although the doctor doesn’t list them together, they are clearly present in the history and collectively represent multiple cardiac risk factors.
Doctor: “We're probably gonna have to call an ambulance for you.” Later: “ambulance team will be with you very shortly.” This indicates immediate activation for urgent hospital evaluation.

Doctor emphasizes: “It's very important that you communicate that to the hospital detail you've just told me because we may need to consider aspirin despite.” This advises patient to inform EMS/hospital about the aspirin allergy.
Doctor: “I'm going to stay on the line with you until they come, okay?” and later: “What I'm going to do is we'll stay on the line for the time being. Until they come.”
Doctor: “once they come, then I'll hand over to them. I'll explain what's going on.” This is a plan to hand over clinical details to EMS.

Consultation is clearly remote (“I can't tell from the video. Are you overweight?”), and there is no documentation of vitals, physical exam, or diagnostic tests, so stating that none are available is accurate.
